picks.title: OpenAI's first gadget sounds like a tiny expressive AI companion
picks.excerpt: OpenAI's first hardware device is reportedly a screenless doughnut-shaped puck you can move room to room, priced around $300 to $400 for a 2027 release. It is the clearest signal yet that the post-phone AI object is being designed as a character, not an interface.
picks.rationale: A screenless, characterful puck is OpenAI betting that the next AI device is industrial design and behaviour rather than UI - the brief that lands on product designers' desks next.

picks.title: LG wants to build humanoid robots, and NVIDIA is giving it the brains
picks.excerpt: LG is moving its CLOiD humanoid from CES concept toward a real product line, with NVIDIA supplying the robotics AI stack. A major appliance maker treating a humanoid as a home-product category changes what domestic industrial design has to solve for.
picks.rationale: The freshest item in the pool, and the moment a mainstream appliance maker treats a humanoid as a home product line - domestic form, safety and affordance questions stop being concept work.

picks.title: New affordable 3-in-1 smart glasses promise up to 39 days of battery and UV protection
picks.excerpt: Rogbid's $69.99 VisionW pairs interchangeable frames with ChatGPT and Grok access, open-ear audio and a claimed 39-day battery. Sub-$100 AI eyewear collapses the price floor that has kept smart glasses a premium-design category.
picks.rationale: A $70 assistant-in-your-frames breaks the price floor that let smart glasses be designed as luxury objects, and interchangeable frames reframe the category as eyewear first, electronics second.

picks.title: Apple Trained Own AI Model for China Market With Help From Alibaba
picks.excerpt: Apple built a separate in-house model, with Alibaba's help, to run Apple Intelligence on iPhones sold in China. Region-specific models mean the same hardware now ships materially different AI behaviour by market.
picks.rationale: Identical hardware now behaves differently by region, so 'the AI feature' stops being one spec and becomes a localisation variable product teams have to design and test per market.

picks.title: I trusted Antigravity and a local LLM with the same office tasks, and only one respected my files
picks.excerpt: A head-to-head of Google's Antigravity agent against a locally hosted LLM on identical document tasks, judged on whether each respected existing files. Agentic AI tools can do the work, but only one kept the user's originals intact.
picks.rationale: The practical test nobody runs before handing an agent a folder: not whether it can do the task, but whether your source files survive it.
